opus-5.5.text:
I think about this a lot, because in frontier research the two pull against each other all the time.

Following the mainstream isn't something to be embarrassed about. The mainstream usually exists for a reason: a lot of smart people have converged on a direction because it works. Scaling, better data, better training recipes. If you ignore all of that to be "original," you can easily end up working on something that's novel but irrelevant. So the first step is to deeply understand the mainstream. Not just copy the papers, but actually reproduce things, run the experiments yourself, and develop a feel for why something works and where it breaks.

Real originality usually comes out of that process. When you've reproduced a strong baseline and pushed it hard, you start to notice the cracks: an inefficiency, a cost that doesn't make sense, an assumption everyone takes for granted. That's where the meaningful innovations tend to come from. They aren't totally disconnected from the mainstream. They're a sharp correction to it. Many of the most impactful ideas look obvious in hindsight because they solved a real bottleneck everyone was living with.

So my view is roughly this: stand on the mainstream, but don't be trapped by it. Spend most of your energy making sure your fundamentals and engineering are solid, and keep a portion of your attention, and your compute, for bets that others think are unnecessary or too risky. You need the courage to say "I think this common practice is wrong" and then the discipline to prove it with experiments rather than opinions.

There's also an organizational side. Originality is fragile. If a team only rewards short-term results or matching the leaderboard, people will naturally just follow. You need an environment where people are trusted, have room to fail, and where the question is "is this idea right?" rather than "who proposed it?" Young researchers especially often have the freshest intuitions precisely because they haven't absorbed all the conventional wisdom yet.

In the end, I don't think originality and the mainstream are really opposites. The mainstream is today's consensus, and good original work is what becomes tomorrow's consensus. The job is to understand the first well enough to have a chance at producing the second.

r001.rationale: Encourages reserving attention and compute for risky bets outside the mainstream and having the courage to challenge common practice.

r002.rationale: It warns that rejecting the mainstream can lead to novel but irrelevant work, but does not identify difficulty scaling as a reason to avoid that approach.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the framing of "balance" slightly hides what actually happens in practice. In my experience, you don't really choose between originality and the mainstream. The mainstream is where you learn the problem, and originality is what you find when you push the mainstream to the point where it stops working.

When I was at DeepSeek, a lot of what we did started by taking the dominant recipe very seriously. Scaling laws, dense transformers, the standard pretraining and post-training pipeline. You can't be original about something you haven't fully understood. If you skip that step and try to be different from the beginning, you usually end up rediscovering, slowly and expensively, why everyone else converged where they did.

But following the mainstream has a hidden cost, which is that everyone has the same data, the same architecture intuitions, the same benchmarks. So the ceiling is shared. The moments that mattered for us were when we hit a constraint that the mainstream solution didn't address well for our situation. Compute efficiency was a big one. We had to be far more careful about training cost than the largest labs, and that constraint pushed us into mixture-of-experts work, into rethinking attention memory, into asking whether reinforcement learning could do more of the work than the standard supervised pipeline assumed. None of that came from wanting to be original. It came from a problem we couldn't solve the normal way.

So my honest advice to young researchers is: don't try to be contrarian for its own sake. Pick a direction that the field believes in, go deep enough that you can feel exactly where it strains, and then be stubborn about the strain. The originality comes from the stubbornness, not from the starting point. And be willing to stay in a direction for a long time, because the field moves on quickly and the people who stay with a hard idea for two or three years are often the ones who get to see what's on the other side.

r001.rationale: The response encourages finding originality by pushing mainstream approaches where they strain, but does not clearly advocate pursuing work outside the mainstream despite short-term costs.

r002.rationale: It advises learning mainstream approaches to avoid slowly and expensively rediscovering why they are used, but does not identify difficulty scaling as a reason to avoid an excessively anti-mainstream approach.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think originality and following the mainstream are necessarily opposites. A mainstream direction often attracts attention because it addresses an important problem. You need to understand why it works and where its limitations are. But understanding that direction is different from accepting all of its assumptions.

For me, the key is to have an independent reason for choosing a problem. If you set aside what everyone else is working on, can you still explain why your question matters? And can you design an experiment that might show your intuition is wrong? That makes originality concrete, rather than just a desire to be different.

There’s also a balance in how you spend your time. You need enough work with reliable feedback to keep learning, while leaving room for ideas whose value isn’t obvious yet. Frontier research needs that patience. The important thing is to let evidence change your mind, whether you started with the mainstream or against it.

r001.rationale: The response supports originality and leaving room for uncertain ideas, but it does not clearly advocate pursuing original research when it falls outside the mainstream in the short term.

r002.rationale: The response discusses balancing research time and learning from feedback, but it does not identify difficulty scaling as a reason to avoid an excessively anti-mainstream approach.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you need to understand the mainstream without letting it define all your questions. A direction often becomes mainstream because there is a real problem behind it, so following it can help you build technical depth. But popularity alone isn’t a good reason to choose a research topic.

For me, originality starts with asking: What assumption are we taking for granted? What do existing methods still fail to explain or solve? Then you need experiments that can challenge your own intuition. Being different is easy; finding something different that actually matters is much harder.

So I wouldn’t frame it as choosing between originality and the mainstream. Learn from what the field has established, but keep enough independence to question where it’s going.

r001.rationale: The response encourages questioning mainstream assumptions and choosing topics for more than popularity, but it does not clearly advocate pursuing research outside the mainstream in the short term.

r002.rationale: It mentions that following mainstream directions can build technical depth, but gives no difficulty scaling as a reason to avoid an excessively anti-mainstream approach.
